items.stem:
Farmer Ramu has a wild rose plant in his garden that has a very strong and disease-resistant root system but produces small, dull flowers. He wants to grow large, beautiful yellow roses instead. He takes a healthy stem piece from a yellow rose plant, carefully makes a slit on a twig of his wild rose plant, and inserts the yellow rose stem into the slit. He then wraps the joint securely with a cotton cloth and plastic film to protect it from pests, watering it regularly until the two parts heal and grow together.
(a) Which specific method of artificial vegetative propagation is Farmer Ramu using?
(b) Why did Ramu wrap the joint with a cotton cloth and plastic film?
(c) What is the central biological process behind this type of reproduction, and how do the new yellow roses genetically compare to the parent yellow rose plant?
items.answer:
(a) Farmer Ramu is using the method of grafting.
(b) He wrapped the joint to avoid pests from entering the graft until it heals completely and to keep the joined area secure and protected.
(c) The central biological process behind this asexual reproduction is mitosis. Because it involves only one parent for the shoot system, the new yellow roses produced will be genetically identical to the parent yellow rose plant, acting as clones.

items.stem:
Before leaving for a week-long family vacation, Rahul accidentally left a slightly moist piece of homemade roti inside a dark steel container on the kitchen counter. When he returned and opened the container, he was surprised to see fuzzy black and grey patches completely covering the roti. Intrigued, he took a small sample to his school laboratory. Under the microscope, he observed a network of thread-like structures with tiny, round sacs at their tips, which contained thousands of minute spherical bodies waiting to be released into the air.
(a) Identify the organism growing on the roti and the specific mode of asexual reproduction it uses.
(b) What are the thread-like structures and the tiny round sacs at their tips called?
(c) Why did the organism grow so rapidly on the roti inside the closed steel container?
(d) How did the organism originally reach the freshly made roti before Rahul left for his vacation?
items.answer:
(a) The organism is bread mould (a type of fungus like Rhizopus), and it reproduces asexually through spore formation.
(b) The thread-like structures are called fungal hyphae, and the tiny round sacs at their tips are called sporangia (or spore sacs).
(c) The organism grew rapidly because the dark, warm, and moist environment inside the steel container provided highly favorable conditions for the spores to germinate and multiply quickly.
(d) Spores of the mould are extremely lightweight and float easily through air currents. They were already present in the kitchen air and settled on the moist roti before the container was closed.

items.stem:
During a science exhibition, 14-year-old Aman was looking at a family photograph. He noticed that while he shares his father’s black hair and his mother’s brown eyes, he looks quite different from his younger sister, who has blonde hair and blue eyes. His biology teacher explained that although human cells generally contain a fixed number of chromosomes, the cells responsible for reproduction undergo a special type of division. This unique division ensures that the chromosome number does not double in every generation and creates a random mixing of genetic traits.
(a) Name the special type of cell division that forms reproductive cells.
(b) How many chromosomes are present in a normal human body cell compared to a human reproductive cell?
(c) What are the male and female reproductive cells (gametes) called in humans?
(d) Compare the human male and female gametes based on their size and motility.
(e) Why is the variation created by this cell division important for a species?
items.answer:
(a) The special type of cell division is called meiosis.
(b) A normal human body cell contains 46 chromosomes, whereas a human reproductive cell (gamete) contains half that number, which is 23 chromosomes.
(c) The male gametes are called sperm, and the female gametes are called eggs (or ova).
(d) Human male gametes (sperm) are very small and actively motile (moving). In contrast, female gametes (eggs) are much larger and non-motile.
(e) Variation helps some individuals within a population adapt better to changing environments, ensuring the long-term survival and evolution of the species.

items.stem:
A group of students decided to conduct an experiment on garden pea plants in their school greenhouse. They selected two juvenile flower buds on the same plant. For the first bud (Bud A), they carefully removed all the stamens and wrapped it loosely in a muslin cloth bag. For the second bud (Bud B), they left all the parts intact but also wrapped it tightly in a muslin cloth bag. They observed both buds regularly for several weeks to check if fruits would develop in place of the flowers.
(a) Why did the students wrap the flower buds in muslin cloth bags?
(b) Predict whether Bud A will develop into a fruit. Justify your answer.
(c) Will Bud B be able to produce a fruit? If yes, through which specific process?
(d) What is the main function of the stamens that were removed from Bud A?
items.answer:
(a) The students wrapped the buds in muslin cloth bags to prevent unwanted pollen grains from external sources (cross-pollination) from reaching the stigma of the flowers.
(b) Bud A will not develop into a fruit. Since its stamens were removed and it was covered, no pollen could reach its stigma, meaning fertilisation cannot take place.
(c) Yes, Bud B will likely produce a fruit. Since its stamens were left intact inside the bag, pollen from its own anthers can fall onto its stigma, leading to self-pollination and subsequent fertilisation.
(d) The main function of the stamen, which is the male reproductive part, is to produce pollen grains that contain the male gametes necessary for reproduction.

items.stem:
An agricultural research center maintains two large fields side by side. Field X grows maize, which produces massive quantities of tiny, lightweight, and dry pollen grains, though its flowers lack bright petals and nectar. Field Y grows sunflowers, featuring large, vibrant yellow petals and heavy, sticky pollen. Recently, aggressive pesticide use in a nearby village caused a severe drop in the local butterfly and bee populations. Within a few weeks, scientists noticed a massive decline in seed formation in one field, while the other remained largely unaffected.
(a) Which field (X or Y) experienced a severe decline in seed formation and why?
(b) What is the pollinating agent for the crop in Field X, and how is its pollen adapted for this?
(c) Explain why producing extremely large numbers of pollen grains is an effective and necessary strategy for the plants in Field X.
items.answer:
(a) Field Y (sunflowers) experienced a severe decline. Sunflowers rely on insects like bees and butterflies for cross-pollination. The pesticide reduced insect populations, preventing pollen transfer.
(b) The pollinating agent for Field X (maize) is the wind. Its pollen is adapted by being very small, lightweight, and dry, allowing it to be easily carried by air currents.
(c) Wind pollination is a highly random and undirected process. A large portion of the pollen blows away and never reaches a female flower. Producing millions of pollen grains increases the probability that at least some will successfully land on a compatible stigma.

items.stem:
During a biology practical, a teacher showed a microscopic video of plant reproduction. The students watched a tiny yellow grain land on the sticky, flattened top of a female floral part. Suddenly, a long tube began to sprout from the yellow grain, pushing its way downwards through a long neck-like passage. The tube eventually reached a swollen base at the bottom, delivering its contents to fuse with a tiny egg cell located inside a small compartment. The teacher explained this fusion is the beginning of a new plant life.
(a) Identify the sticky flattened top, the long neck-like passage, and the swollen base of the female floral part.
(b) What is the yellow grain, and what is the tube growing from it called?
(c) Name the process of fusion between the contents of the tube and the egg cell. What is the newly formed cell called?
(d) What will the swollen base and the tiny egg compartments eventually develop into after this process is complete?
(e) Mention two common agents that help in the dispersal of the final reproductive structures in nature.
items.answer:
(a) The sticky flattened top is the stigma, the long neck-like passage is the style, and the swollen base is the ovary.
(b) The yellow grain is a pollen grain, and the tube growing from it is the pollen tube.
(c) The fusion process is called fertilisation. The newly formed cell is called a zygote.
(d) The swollen base (ovary) will develop into a fruit, and the tiny egg compartments (ovules) will develop into seeds.
(e) Seed dispersal commonly takes place by wind, water, or animals.

items.stem:
A nature documentary contrasts the life cycles of two different animals. First, it shows a female salmon fish in a shallow stream releasing thousands of soft, transparent eggs directly into the water, while a male salmon swims over them, releasing a cloudy fluid. Next, the camera moves to a nearby tree where a female pigeon lays just two hard-shelled eggs in a carefully woven nest. The narrator explains that the pigeon’s eggs were already fertilized deep inside her body before the protective shells were formed around them.
(a) Differentiate between the modes of fertilisation exhibited by the salmon fish and the pigeon.
(b) Why does the salmon fish need to produce thousands of eggs while the pigeon produces only two?
(c) Where does the developing embryo inside the pigeon’s egg get its nutrition from?
(d) Which of the two animals ensures a higher estimated survival rate of its young ones and why?
items.answer:
(a) The salmon fish exhibits external fertilisation, where gametes fuse outside the body in water. The pigeon exhibits internal fertilisation, where gametes fuse inside the female’s body.
(b) The salmon produces thousands of eggs because many are destroyed by water currents or eaten by predators, so a large number ensures at least a few survive. The pigeon produces fewer eggs because internal fertilisation and hard shells offer better protection.
(c) The developing embryo inside the pigeon’s egg gets its nutrition from the yolk, which contains nutritive substances stored specifically to nourish it until it hatches.
(d) The pigeon ensures a higher survival rate. Internal fertilisation, protective eggshells, and parental care in a nest protect the offspring from harsh environmental conditions and predators compared to the unprotected fish eggs in open water.

items.stem:
Dr. Mehta is counseling a young couple about reproductive biology using anatomical charts. He points to a diagram of the male system, highlighting two oval-shaped structures resting in a pouch outside the main body cavity, explaining their critical role in generating millions of motile cells and hormones. He then switches to the female chart, tracing how a single mature egg is released from one of the almond-shaped organs each month. The egg then travels into a narrow, funnel-like tube where it waits to potentially meet the male gametes.
(a) Name the oval-shaped structures in the male body and the pouch they rest in.
(b) Why are these male reproductive structures located in a pouch outside the main abdominal cavity?
(c) Identify the almond-shaped organs in the female that produce the egg, and the narrow tube the egg travels into.
(d) How do the secretions from glands like the seminal vesicles and prostate assist the male gametes?
items.answer:
(a) The oval-shaped structures are the testes, and they rest in a pouch called the scrotum.
(b) They are located outside the abdominal cavity because the scrotum keeps the testes at a temperature slightly cooler than normal body temperature, which is necessary for the proper production of sperm.
(c) The almond-shaped organs are the ovaries, and the narrow tube the egg travels into is the oviduct (or fallopian tube).
(d) The secretions from the seminal vesicles and prostate gland add nourishing fluids that help the sperm remain active and make it easier for them to move and swim towards the egg.

items.stem:
Anita attended an adolescent health seminar at her school. The guest speaker, a gynecologist, explained the rhythmic biological cycle that a female body undergoes starting from puberty. She described how the inner lining of a pear-shaped, bag-like organ gradually thickens and enriches with blood vessels in anticipation of receiving a developing embryo. She further explained that if the mature egg released halfway through the cycle does not encounter a sperm, this thickened lining is no longer needed and breaks down, leaving the body naturally.
(a) What is the pear-shaped, bag-like organ called, and what event marks the beginning of pregnancy in this organ?
(b) What is the process of releasing a mature egg halfway through the cycle called, and roughly on which day of a typical 28-day cycle does it occur?
(c) What is the scientific term for the breakdown and exit of the thickened lining and blood, and how long does this phase usually last?
items.answer:
(a) The organ is called the uterus. The beginning of pregnancy is marked by implantation, which is when the developing zygote embeds into the thickened inner lining of the uterus.
(b) The process is called ovulation, and it typically occurs around the 14th day of a 28-day menstrual cycle.
(c) The scientific term is menstruation. This shedding phase usually lasts for 3 to 7 days.

items.stem:
A local health worker, Sunita, conducts a community awareness camp for young adults. She discusses the responsibilities of sexual maturity, emphasizing that physical readiness does not equal emotional readiness. Sunita highlights the importance of safe practices, warning the audience about severe infections that can spread through close physical contact. She displays various family planning tools, specifically pointing out a simple barrier device that is unique because it not only prevents unwanted pregnancies by blocking sperm from reaching the egg but also serves as the primary defense against these serious infections.
(a) Explain the difference between physical sexual maturity and emotional maturity as discussed by Sunita.
(b) What are the severe infections spread through close physical contact called? Give any two examples.
(c) Name the specific barrier device Sunita is pointing out that offers dual protection.
(d) Apart from barrier methods, name one intra-uterine device (IUD) used to avoid pregnancy and state a potential drawback of its use.
items.answer:
(a) Physical sexual maturity means the body is capable of reproduction (producing gametes). Emotional maturity takes longer and involves handling feelings, communicating clearly, and making thoughtful, responsible decisions.
(b) These infections are called Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs). Examples include gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes, genital warts, and HIV/AIDS.
(c) The barrier device offering dual protection is the condom.
(d) An example of an intra-uterine device is the copper-T. A potential drawback is that it may sometimes irritate the uterus and cause discomfort.
